newsitem.title: USA: NASDR urges SEC reject firm's pay-to-play appeal.
newsitem.headline: NASDR urges SEC reject firm's pay-to-play appeal.

text.p: NASD Regulation (NASDR) warned the Securities and Exchange Commission on Tuesday that SEC could "significantly undermine" municipal bond pay-to-play rule G-37 if it grants Morgan Stanley an exemption.

The National Association of Securities Dealers regulatory arm, in a 24-page brief filed with SEC, also said that Morgan Stanley Dean Witter Discover & Co. had already won an exemption from rule G-37 in fall 1994 for a different matter. Another exemption is unwarranted, it said.
Enacted in April 1994, rule G-37 bars dealers who make contributions to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments.

Morgan Stanley last winter requested an exemption from the two-year ban after managing director Peter Karches made a $1,000 contribution in September 1996 to the U.S. Senate campaign of William Weld, who was governor of Massachusetts.
Thomas Casella, vice president of NASDR's compliance department, denied the request in December 1996, saying the firm did not present an adequate excuse.
Karches is a member of the firm's management committee and head of its fixed income division.
NASDR said Karches did not preclear the contribution with the firm, which discovered it during a routine review of 6,000 employees.
Karches, who said he thought a contribution to a candidate for federal office was permissible under G-37, got a refund of the donation within 24 hours, NASDR said.
After Cassella rejected Morgan Stanley's request, the firm on Jan. 2, 1997 appealed to NASDR's fixed income committee, which upheld the ruling in February. Morgan Stanley then appealed to SEC.
NASDR warned in its brief that granting an exemption could trigger many more requests similar to Morgan Stanley's, watering down considerably the rule's effectiveness.
It also warned that a recent decision by SEC to temporarily lift rule G-37's two-year ban in Morgan Stanley's case impairs the purpose of rule G-37, which is to protect investors.

NASDR noted that in fall 1994, the firm learned that a managing director had made a $1,000 contribution to the campaign of Bruce Benson, a candidate for Governor of Colorado. Morgan Stanley requested an exemption in November 1994 and NASD granted the request.
"The firm should have been alerted to the fact that it had not educated its municipal finance professionals sufficiently to ensure compliance with the Rule," NASDR said in its brief.
"A thorough review of its compliance policy would have shown errors and omissions in the firm's initial communications with employees regarding the Rule," NASDR said.
A Morgan Stanley spokesperson said the firm's brief in the case will be available in the SEC's public reference room.
